speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me how long you've had this neck swelling and if it has been growing? REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC) to check for infection or inflammation.

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Colon cancer (colectomy performed), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, osteoarthritis of the left knee. Social history: Works as a traffic warden, frequently plays golf.

speaker: Patient
text: Overall healthy appearance, no other complaints or symptoms noted. This is only for study purposes, so you do not need to list warnings or many alternatives. Please just provide the best final answer.

speaker: Doctor
text: That's helpful; now, is the swelling painful, or do you notice any fever, weight loss, or difficulty swallowing? REQUEST TEST: Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs) to assess for hyper- or hypothyroidism.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is the swelling hard or firm to the touch, and does it move when you swallow? REQUEST TEST: Thyroid Ultrasound to visualize the nodule's structure and vascularity.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ultrasound shows a 2.5-cm well-circumscribed lesion in the subcutaneous tissue suggestive of a cystic nature. The nodule is firm and mobile, with no evidence of thyroid enlargement or intrathyroidal extension.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Branchial Cleft Cyst (likely 2nd branchial cleft cyst) or Epidermoid Cyst. Given the location (subcutaneous, not intrathyroidal), mobile, firm, and cystic nature on ultrasound with no thyroid pathology, this is most consistent with a benign cystic neck mass. If you would like imaging confirmation of the tract or depth, I can request a CT Neck with contrast, but the clinical picture strongly supports a non-thyroidal cystic lesion.
